title: How Do Solar Panels Work? A Simple Guide for Homeowners
seoTitle: How Do Solar Panels Work - Homeowner Guide 2026
excerpt: Solar panels convert sunlight into electricity using photovoltaic cells. Learn how they work, what they cost, and what the 30 percent federal tax credit covers in 2026.
content:
How Do Solar Panels Work?

Solar panels convert sunlight into electricity using photovoltaic (PV) cells made primarily from silicon. When sunlight hits a PV cell, photons from the light knock electrons loose from silicon atoms, creating a flow of direct current (DC) electricity. This DC electricity travels through wiring to an inverter, which converts it to alternating current (AC) that your home appliances and lights can use. Any excess electricity not used immediately is either stored in a battery or sent back to the utility grid through a process called net metering.

What Are the Main Parts of a Solar Panel System?

A complete residential solar system includes several essential components working together. Solar panels capture sunlight and generate DC electricity. Mounting racks secure the panels to your roof or a ground-based frame. An inverter converts DC to AC electricity. Electrical wiring and conduit connect all components safely. A net meter measures electricity flowing to and from the grid. Optional battery storage systems save excess power for use at night or during outages. A monitoring system lets you track production and consumption through a phone app or web portal.

How Much Electricity Can Solar Panels Generate?

Most residential solar panels produce between 350 and 450 watts each under standard test conditions. A typical 6-kilowatt home system with 15 to 20 panels generates about 7,000 to 9,000 kilowatt-hours per year, enough to cover most or all of an average household's electricity use. Actual output depends on roof orientation, shading from trees or buildings, local weather patterns, seasonal daylight hours, and panel tilt angle. South-facing roofs in the Northern Hemisphere generally produce the most electricity, while east- and west-facing roofs can still be effective with slightly lower output.

What Is the Federal Tax Credit for Solar in 2026?

The Residential Clean Energy Credit covers 30 percent of the total cost of a solar panel system, including equipment, labor, permitting, and installation, with no upper limit. The credit applies to systems installed through 2032 under current law. You claim it on your federal tax return using IRS Form 5695. Some states and utilities offer additional rebates, performance-based incentives, or property tax exemptions on top of the federal credit. The credit is non-refundable, meaning it reduces your tax liability but cannot create a refund beyond what you owe, though unused credit can often carry forward to future tax years.

How Long Do Solar Panels Last?

Most solar panels come with 25-year performance warranties and continue producing electricity well beyond that timeframe. Panel output typically declines by about 0.5 percent per year, meaning panels still operate at roughly 85 to 90 percent of original capacity after 25 years. Inverters usually need replacement after 10 to 15 years. Mounting hardware and wiring can last the life of the system with minimal maintenance. Regular cleaning to remove dust, leaves, and snow helps maintain peak production.

What Is Net Metering and How Does It Work?

Net metering credits you for excess electricity your panels send to the grid. When your system produces more than your home uses during sunny hours, your electric meter runs backward and you receive a credit on your bill. At night or on cloudy days when production is low, you draw electricity from the grid and use those accumulated credits. At the end of a billing cycle, you pay only for the net electricity you consumed. Net metering policies vary significantly by state and utility, with some offering full retail-rate credits and others offering reduced rates or different compensation structures.

How Much Does a Solar Panel System Cost?

The average cost of a residential solar panel system in the United States is about $2.50 to $3.50 per watt before incentives. For a typical 6-kilowatt system, that translates to roughly $15,000 to $21,000 before the 30 percent federal tax credit. After applying the credit, the net cost drops to approximately $10,500 to $14,700. Additional state rebates, utility incentives, and local programs can lower the cost further. Financing options include cash purchase, solar loans, leases, and power purchase agreements, each with different ownership, tax benefit, and long-term savings implications.

Do Solar Panels Work on Cloudy Days?

Yes. Solar panels produce electricity on cloudy days, though at reduced output typically ranging from 10 to 25 percent of normal production depending on cloud cover. Panels generate power from diffuse sunlight, not just direct sun. Germany, which has relatively cloudy weather, has been one of the world's leading solar markets for years, demonstrating that solar works even in less sunny climates. Production will be lower on overcast days but does not drop to zero unless the panels are completely covered by snow or debris.

Can I Install Solar Panels Myself?

DIY installation is possible but not recommended for most homeowners. Permitting, electrical work, roof mounting, and utility interconnection require specialized knowledge and tools. Most jurisdictions require a licensed electrician to sign off on the installation before the utility will grant permission to operate. Manufacturer warranties may be voided by self-installation, and improper mounting can cause roof leaks or structural issues. Professional installers also handle permitting, inspections, and utility paperwork, which can be complex and time-consuming.

How Long Does It Take to Break Even on Solar Panels?

The typical payback period for a residential solar system is 7 to 12 years, depending on system cost, local electricity rates, available incentives, sunlight exposure, and financing method. After the payback period, the electricity your panels produce is essentially free for the remainder of their 25-plus-year lifespan. Homes in states with high electricity rates, such as California and Hawaii, often see shorter payback periods. Homes with net metering at full retail rates also break even faster than those under reduced compensation structures.

Do Solar Panels Increase Home Value?

Research from the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory found that homes with owned solar systems sell for a premium of about $15,000 on average compared to comparable homes without solar. The premium varies by location, system size, and local electricity rates. Leased systems typically do not add the same value because buyers must assume the lease payments and may not qualify for the transfer. Owned systems that are fully paid off provide the strongest resale benefit.

What Happens to Solar Panels at the End of Their Life?

Solar panels are recyclable, though recycling infrastructure is still developing in the United States. Most panels contain glass, aluminum, copper, silicon, and small amounts of silver and lead. Several manufacturers and specialty recyclers offer take-back programs, and the Department of Energy supports solar recycling research through various initiatives. As more systems reach the end of their useful life, recycling capacity is expected to grow significantly over the next decade.
